params.question: During a right adrenalectomy, the adrenal vein poses a particular surgical hazard. What makes the right adrenal vein more dangerous than the left?

answers.text: It crosses anterior to the IVC, requiring retraction of a major vessel during dissection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The right adrenal vein does not cross anterior to the IVC — it drains directly into the IVC posterolaterally. Its danger lies in its short length and the catastrophic consequences of a tear at the IVC junction.

answers.text: It is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava, risking severe haemorrhage if injured

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The right adrenal vein is short and empties directly into the IVC. A tear at this junction causes rapid, hard-to-control bleeding — hence surgeons call it the 'treacherous vein.'

answers.text: It is longer and more tortuous than the left, making it prone to tearing during mobilisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. It is the left adrenal vein that is longer. The right adrenal vein is short, which is precisely what makes it dangerous — there is almost no margin for error during dissection.

answers.text: It shares a common trunk with the right renal vein, complicating safe ligation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The right adrenal vein drains independently into the IVC, not via the renal vein. It is the left adrenal vein that drains into the left renal vein.

overallFeedback.feedback: The right adrenal vein is called the 'treacherous vein' because it is short and empties directly into the IVC. Even a small tear causes severe bleeding with almost no margin for error. The left side is safer because its vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein.

Correct! The right adrenal vein is short and drains directly into the IVC — a tear means rapid, hard-to-control haemorrhage. The left adrenal vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein, giving the surgeon more working room.

params.question: Why must phaeochromocytoma be excluded biochemically before performing a percutaneous biopsy of any adrenal mass?

answers.text: Because manipulating a phaeochromocytoma can trigger a life-threatening catecholamine surge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! A phaeochromocytoma stores large quantities of catecholamines. Needle manipulation can provoke massive release, causing a potentially fatal hypertensive and cardiac crisis.

answers.text: Because phaeochromocytoma tissue is highly vascular and causes excessive bleeding on needle biopsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While phaeochromocytomas are vascular, the primary danger is not haemorrhage but the massive catecholamine discharge triggered by mechanical manipulation of the tumour.

answers.text: Because the histological appearance of phaeochromocytoma is indistinguishable from adenoma on core biopsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The concern is not a diagnostic limitation — it is the physiological consequence. Manipulating an unsuspected phaeochromocytoma can trigger a catecholamine crisis before a histological diagnosis is ever made.

answers.text: Because phaeochromocytoma cells can seed along the needle tract, causing extra-adrenal paragangliomas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Needle-tract seeding is a concern with some malignancies, but it is not the reason phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before biopsy. The danger is an acute catecholamine storm.

overallFeedback.feedback: Sampling an unsuspected phaeochromocytoma can trigger massive catecholamine release and a life-threatening hypertensive crisis. Plasma metanephrines must always be measured to rule out phaeochromocytoma before any needle enters an adrenal mass.

Correct! Mechanical manipulation of a phaeochromocytoma releases stored catecholamines, risking a life-threatening crisis. This is why biochemical exclusion (plasma metanephrines) must precede any invasive procedure on an adrenal mass.

interactions.label: A patient with confirmed phaeochromocytoma is being prepared for adrenalectomy.

params.question: A patient with confirmed phaeochromocytoma is being prepared for adrenalectomy. Blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg and heart rate is 116/min. What is the correct pharmacological preparation?

answers.text: Start a beta-blocker immediately to control the tachycardia, then introduce an alpha-blocker for blood pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect and dangerous. Beta-blockade without prior alpha-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction completely unopposed, which can precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis.

answers.text: Administer combined alpha and beta blockade simultaneously from the outset

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Simultaneous initiation risks effective beta-blockade before alpha-blockade is established. The resulting unopposed alpha stimulation can trigger a dangerous hypertensive crisis.

answers.text: Use a calcium channel blocker alone, reserving adrenergic blockade for intraoperative use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While calcium channel blockers have a secondary role, the cornerstone of preoperative phaeochromocytoma preparation is alpha-blockade for 10–14 days to control blood pressure and re-expand intravascular volume.

answers.text: Start an alpha-blocker such as phenoxybenzamine for 10–14 days; add a beta-blocker only if tachycardia persists after adequate alpha-blockade

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Alpha-blockade runs for 10–14 days to control blood pressure and re-expand the contracted blood volume. A beta-blocker is added only after adequate alpha-blockade is established, and only if tachycardia persists.

overallFeedback.feedback: Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker) must always precede beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma. It runs for 10–14 days before surgery. Starting beta first leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed, risking a severe hypertensive crisis.

Correct! Alpha-blockade first, for 10–14 days, to control hypertension and restore intravascular volume. A beta-blocker is added only afterwards, and only if tachycardia persists. Reversing this order risks a life-threatening hypertensive crisis.
